title: Amplitude mode in Eliashberg superconductors
abstract: In the BCS theory of superconductivity the amplitude (Higgs) mode is degenerate with the pair-breaking threshold: its frequency coincides with $2Δ$, so it is an edge singularity rather than a true collective mode. This is why after a sudden weak perturbation at $t=0$ its oscillations decay algebraically as $1/\sqrt{t}$. We show that the retardation effects due to the phonon dynamics in the strong-coupling theory lift this degeneracy. The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge $2Δ_g$, set by the spectral gap, and becomes a sharp subgap excitation. We determine its frequency from the longitudinal pair susceptibility evaluated directly on the real frequency axis, using the Eilenberger equations for Migdal--Eliashberg theory with the Einstein phonon spectrum. The response of the mass renormalization supplies at least two fifths of the displacement, and possibly all of it: with it switched off, the binding falls below the resolution of the calculation. Its consequences, however, are significant because a percent-level shift transfers about a quarter of the spectral weight of the amplitude channel out of the two-quasiparticle continuum into a discrete energy level. What experiment sees is therefore not the displacement itself but its consequence: amplitude oscillations that persist instead of decaying as $1/\sqrt{t}$.
summary: This paper investigates the Higgs amplitude mode in strongly coupled superconductors, showing that phonon retardation effects lift the mode's degeneracy from the pair-breaking threshold. Using the Eilenberger equations on the real frequency axis, the authors predict the mode becomes a sharp, undamped subgap excitation, causing a measurable transfer of spectral weight from the continuum.
main_problem: To determine if retardation effects from phonon dynamics in strong-coupling superconductors lift the degeneracy of the amplitude (Higgs) mode from the pair-breaking threshold ($2\Delta_g$).
main_result: The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge, becoming a sharp subgap excitation with a binding energy predicted to be $2\Delta_g - \omega_H = 0.028 \Delta_g^2/\Omega$ in the intermediate-coupling regime.
method: The frequency is determined by evaluating the longitudinal pair susceptibility directly on the real frequency axis using the Eilenberger equations within the Migdal-Eliashberg theory framework.
model_or_system: The study focuses on superconductors described by a complex order parameter, utilizing the Migdal–Eliashberg theory with an Einstein phonon spectrum to model strong electron-phonon coupling.
key_observables: Amplitude mode frequency ($\omega_H$), spectral weight transfer, and the time-domain oscillation signature.
important_parameters: Intermediate-coupling window ($0.56 \le \Delta_g/\Omega \le 0.90$), the ratio $\Delta_g/\Omega$, and the gap edge $2\Delta_g$.
main_assumptions: The calculation requires using the real-axis Eilenberger-Keldysh approach, as the imaginary axis calculation fails to resolve the necessary small energy shifts.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the time-domain signature, contrasting the BCS prediction of $t^{-1/2}$ decay with the predicted undamped pole, and showing the spectral weight transferred from the continuum to the discrete level.
paper_structure: The paper contrasts the BCS prediction (algebraic decay) with the strong-coupling prediction (detachment). It details the theoretical machinery using Eilenberger equations on the real axis to locate the pole, derives the quantitative binding energy formula, and discusses the physical consequence of spectral weight redistribution.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed, quantitative theoretical prediction for a collective mode in superconductors, linking microscopic electron-phonon coupling effects to observable spectral weight changes, which is highly relevant to understanding pairing mechanisms beyond simple BCS theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Time-domain signature of the amplitude mode. Left panel: spectral function of the longitudinal pair susceptibility χ(ω)/χ(0). The pole corresponding to amplitude Higgs mode then holds approximately 25% of it. Shading marks the continuum weight that retardation removes from the neighborhood of the edge. We depict the weight transferred from the edge into the pole by the shaded area. Right panel: order-parameter amplitude after a sudden weak pair field applied at t = 0, in units of its new equilibrium value, computed at that binding. The BCS oscillation dephases across the continuum with envelope ∝t−1/2 (dashed). The pole gives an undamped oscillation of relative amplitude 0.265...

FIG. 4. Isolating the mass-renormalization response in the longitudinal pair propagator. Normalized inverse propagator χ−1 Φ (iνl)/χ−1 Φ (0) at four couplings. Solid: the full system (24). Dashed: the same system with δW ≡0, i.e. with the vertex re- tardation acting alone. The gap between the two curves is the mass-renormalization response. The full system’s curve rises faster with νl: the mass channel lowers χ−1 Φ near νl = 0 relative to its high-frequency value, which is the imaginary-axis signature of the additional attraction in the amplitude channel discussed in the text; removing δW moves the mode towards the threshold. N = 1024, T/Ω= 0.005.
